back: The branch of biology that deals with inheritance as well as the variation of characters from parents to offspring.
The process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny; it is the basis of heredity.
The degree by which progeny differ from their parents.
A line that, after continuous self-pollination, shows stable trait inheritance and expression for several generations.
The unit of inheritance. It contains the information required to express a particular trait in an organism; Mendel called it a factor.
Genes which code for a pair of contrasting traits, i.e. slightly different forms of the same gene. Capital letter for the F1 trait, small letter for the other.
Genotype is the allelic constitution of the organism (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype is the visible expression of that constitution (tall or dwarf).
Homozygous means both alleles are identical (TT or tt) and the plant breeds true; heterozygous means the alleles differ (Tt) and two kinds of gametes are formed.
A cross between two plants that differ in one pair of contrasting characters, e.g. TT x tt. The F1 is Tt and the F2 gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf.

A graphical representation, devised by Reginald C. Punnett, to calculate the probability of all possible genotypes of offspring in a genetic cross; gametes are written along the top row and left column.

Characters are controlled by discrete units called factors; factors occur in pairs; in a dissimilar pair one member dominates the other. It explains why only one parental character appears in the F1 and both appear in a 3 : 1 ratio in the F2.
The alleles of a pair segregate from each other during gamete formation so that a gamete receives only one of the two factors. Alleles do not blend, so both characters are recovered in the F2.

Crossing an organism showing the dominant phenotype, whose genotype is to be determined, with the recessive parent instead of self-crossing. An all-dominant progeny means homozygous; a 1 : 1 ratio means heterozygous.
The F1 has a phenotype in between the two parents. Example: snapdragon RR red x rr white gives Rr pink, and the F2 is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so the phenotypic ratio equals the genotypic ratio.
The F1 resembles both parents at once because each allele expresses its own product. Example: ABO blood group, where IAIB red cells carry both A and B sugars.

More than two alleles governing the same character in a population, as with IA, IB and i of the ABO gene. An individual carries only two of them, so multiple alleles are seen only in population studies.

The normal allele makes a functional enzyme that transforms substrate S; a modified allele may make a less efficient enzyme, a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme. The functioning allele is dominant, the modified one usually recessive.
When two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair. It gives four gamete types in equal numbers and a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 F2 ratio.
9 round yellow : 3 wrinkled yellow : 3 round green : 1 wrinkled green, obtained as (3 round : 1 wrinkled) x (3 yellow : 1 green).

Proposed by Sutton and Boveri: the pairing and separation of a pair of chromosomes leads to the segregation of the pair of factors they carry. Chromosomes and genes both occur in pairs and behave in parallel.
The physical association of two or more genes on the same chromosome, which keeps parental combinations together and raises their proportion above the non-parental types.
The generation of non-parental gene combinations. Its frequency measures the distance between genes on a chromosome, and was used by Sturtevant to build genetic maps.
White and yellow: 1.3 per cent (tightly linked, close together). White and miniature wing: 37.2 per cent (loosely linked, farther apart).

A trait controlled by three or more genes in which the effect of each allele is additive, giving a continuous gradient. Examples: human height and skin colour; the environment also influences the phenotype.
A single gene exhibiting multiple phenotypic expressions, usually because it acts on a metabolic pathway shared by different tissues. Example: phenylketonuria.
A phenomenon that results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently in changes in the genotype and phenotype of an organism.
A change in a single base pair of DNA. Classical example: sickle-cell anaemia, where the sixth codon of the beta globin gene changes from GAG to GUG.
A chemical or physical factor that induces mutation; ultraviolet radiation is a mutagen.
The analysis of traits in several generations of a family, represented as a family tree over generations. It is used to trace the inheritance of a trait, abnormality or disease in human beings.

Disorders determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene, transmitted like any inherited trait. Examples: haemophilia, cystic fibrosis, sickle-cell anaemia, colour blindness, phenylketonuria, thalassemia.
An X-linked recessive defect of the red or green cone of the eye, so red and green cannot be discriminated. About 8 per cent of males and 0.4 per cent of females are affected.

An X-linked recessive disease in which one protein of the blood clotting cascade is affected, so a simple cut causes non-stop bleeding. Carrier females transmit it to some sons; Queen Victoria was a carrier.
An autosomal recessive trait controlled by HbA and HbS. HbS HbS is diseased, HbA HbS is an unaffected carrier. Glu is replaced by Val at position 6 of the beta globin chain (GAG to GUG).
An autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism: the enzyme converting phenylalanine to tyrosine is lacking, so phenylalanine accumulates as phenylpyruvic acid and causes mental retardation.
An autosomal recessive disease of reduced globin chain synthesis, causing anaemia. Alpha thalassemia involves HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16; beta thalassemia involves HBB on chromosome 11.
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem — too few globin molecules are made. Sickle-cell anaemia is a qualitative problem — an incorrectly functioning globin is made.
Aneuploidy is the gain or loss of a chromosome due to failure of chromatid segregation. Polyploidy is an increase in a whole set of chromosomes due to failure of cytokinesis, often seen in plants.

Trisomy of chromosome 21, karyotype 47. Short stature, small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad palm with a characteristic crease, and retarded development. First described by Langdon Down in 1866.
Karyotype 47, XXY, due to an additional X chromosome. Overall masculine development with gynaecomastia; the individual is sterile.
Karyotype 45, X0, due to the absence of one X chromosome. The female is sterile with rudimentary ovaries and lacks secondary sexual characters.

XY type: females are XX and produce only X ova; males are XY and produce 50 per cent X and 50 per cent Y sperms. The sperm therefore decides the sex of the child, with a 50 per cent chance of either sex in each pregnancy.
Females are diploid with 32 chromosomes and develop from fertilised eggs; drones are haploid with 16 chromosomes and develop from unfertilised eggs by parthenogenesis. Drones make sperms by mitosis.
Male heterogamety: the male produces two kinds of gametes (XO in grasshopper, XY in humans and Drosophila). Female heterogamety: the female produces two kinds of gametes (ZW in birds, males ZZ).

Stem height (tall/dwarf), flower colour (violet/white), flower position (axial/terminal), pod shape (inflated/constricted), pod colour (green/yellow), seed shape (round/wrinkled), seed colour (yellow/green).
